bpc-157.chemDesc: Pentadecapeptide fragment of human Body Protection Compound. Sequence: GEPPPGKPADDAGLV. Stable gastric pentadecapeptide; resistant to enzymatic hydrolysis in gastric juice.

tb-500.chemDesc: Synthetic analogue of the actin-sequestering protein Thymosin β-4. 43-amino acid peptide. Promotes actin polymerisation and cellular migration in vitro.

wolverine.chemDesc: Proprietary dual-peptide lyophilised blend. Contains BPC-157 (CAS 137525-51-0) and TB-500 (CAS 77591-33-4) in a fixed molar ratio. Each component independently verified by HPLC.

retatrutide.chemDesc: Triple incretin receptor agonist (GIP-R / GLP-1R / GCGR). C18 fatty diacid-conjugated peptide enabling extended half-life via albumin binding. Investigational compound.

ipamorelin.chemDesc: Pentapeptide growth hormone secretagogue. Selective GHSR-1a agonist. Contains Aib (α-aminoisobutyric acid) at position 1 conferring proteolytic stability.

cjc-1295-dac.chemDesc: Modified GHRH analogue with Drug Affinity Complex (DAC) technology. Covalent albumin binding via maleimide–thiol reaction extends plasma half-life to approximately 6–8 days.

ghk-cu.chemDesc: Copper(II) chelate of the tripeptide glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine. Endogenous plasma peptide. Cu²⁺ coordination via imidazole nitrogen of His and ε-amino group of Lys.

glow-ghk-cu.chemDesc: High-concentration GHK-Cu formulation (70 mg/vial). Identical molecular structure to standard GHK-Cu (CAS 49557-75-7). Elevated dose per vial for intensive in vitro protocols.

nad.chemDesc: Oxidised form of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide. Essential coenzyme in cellular redox reactions. Substrate for sirtuins (SIRT1–7), PARP enzymes, and CD38 NADase.

bacteriostatic-water.chemDesc: Water for injection preserved with 0.9% w/v benzyl alcohol (CAS 100-51-6). Bacteriostatic agent inhibits microbial growth. Suitable for multi-dose reconstitution of lyophilised peptides.
bacteriostatic-water.storage: Store at 15–25 °C; discard 28 days after first use

tirzepatide.chemDesc: Dual incretin receptor agonist (GIP-R / GLP-1R). 39-amino acid peptide with Aib substitution at position 2. C20 fatty diacid moiety enables once-weekly dosing via albumin binding.
tirzepatide.sequence: Dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist peptide — C20 fatty diacid conjugate

epithalon.chemDesc: Synthetic tetrapeptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly). Analogue of epithalamin, a polypeptide isolated from bovine pineal gland. Reported to stimulate telomerase activity in somatic cells in vitro.

ss-31.chemDesc: Szeto-Schiller tetrapeptide. Mitochondria-targeted antioxidant peptide. Selectively concentrates in the inner mitochondrial membrane via electrostatic interaction with cardiolipin.

mk-677-ibutamoren.chemDesc: Non-peptide ghrelin receptor agonist. Orally active GH secretagogue. Selectively mimics the action of endogenous ghrelin at the GHSR-1a receptor.

rad-140-testolone.chemDesc: Nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM). High binding affinity for androgen receptor (AR). Tissue-selective agonist activity in skeletal muscle and bone.

yk-11-myostine.chemDesc: Steroidal SARM and partial agonist of the androgen receptor. Inhibits myostatin (GDF-8) signalling pathway. Structurally derived from 5α-dihydrotestosterone (DHT).

lgd-4033-ligandrol.chemDesc: Nonsteroidal SARM with high oral bioavailability. Selective agonist at androgen receptor in muscle and bone tissue. Fluorinated pyrrolidinyl-benzonitrile scaffold.

mk-2866-ostarine.chemDesc: Nonsteroidal SARM. Arylpropionamide-class androgen receptor ligand. Demonstrates high selectivity for muscle and bone AR over prostate tissue in preclinical models.

gw-501516-cardarine.chemDesc: PPARδ (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor delta) agonist. Thiazole-based synthetic ligand. Activates fatty acid oxidation pathways in skeletal muscle cell lines.

mots-c-uk-mitochondrial-derived-research.chemDesc:
MOTS-c 40mg UK | Mitochondrial-Derived Research Peptide | HPLC Verified | £59.95

Product Overview

MOTS-c 40mg is a mitochondrial-derived research peptide attracting scientific interest for its potential role in cellular energy regulation, metabolic signalling and mitochondrial-to-nuclear communication.

Encoded within the mitochondrial genome, MOTS-c is a 16-amino-acid peptide investigated for its relationship with AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), glucose metabolism, insulin sensitivity and metabolic homeostasis.

Research has explored how MOTS-c may influence cellular responses to metabolic stress and the pathways involved in energy utilisation. These findings have established MOTS-c as an emerging subject in mitochondrial biology and experimental metabolic research.

Research-Chem.uk MOTS-c 40mg is supplied strictly for laboratory research and analytical purposes. The product's reported purity and analytical characteristics should be verified against the relevant batch-specific Certificate of Analysis (COA).

Product Highlights

Product: MOTS-c

Quantity: 40mg

Price: £59.95

Compound class: Mitochondrial-derived peptide

Peptide length: 16 amino acids

Research focus: Mitochondrial signalling and metabolic regulation

Documentation: Refer to the applicable batch-specific COA

Intended use: Laboratory research and analytical purposes only

What Is MOTS-c?

MOTS-c stands for mitochondrial open reading frame of the 12S rRNA-c. First characterised in 2015, it is a short peptide encoded by a region of mitochondrial DNA.

Mitochondria are best known for their role in cellular energy production, but research increasingly recognises their importance in cellular signalling. Mitochondrial-derived peptides such as MOTS-c are being investigated for their potential role in communicating metabolic information between mitochondria and other cellular systems.

Unlike conventional peptides encoded by nuclear DNA, MOTS-c originates from the mitochondrial genome. This distinctive origin makes it particularly relevant to research examining mitochondrial function, metabolic adaptation and cellular homeostasis.

Scientific investigations have explored MOTS-c in relation to:

AMPK-associated signalling pathways

Glucose utilisation and metabolic regulation

Insulin sensitivity in experimental models

Cellular energy homeostasis

Skeletal muscle metabolism

Responses to metabolic stress

Mitochondrial-to-nuclear communication

Age-associated metabolic changes

Although these areas have generated considerable scientific interest, MOTS-c remains investigational. Findings from cell-based and animal studies should not be interpreted as proof of equivalent effects in humans.

How Is MOTS-c Investigated in Research?

One of the principal areas of interest in MOTS-c research is its relationship with AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), an enzyme that functions as a cellular energy sensor.

AMPK helps coordinate metabolic processes in response to changes in cellular energy availability. It participates in pathways associated with glucose utilisation, lipid metabolism and energy balance.

In foundational preclinical research, MOTS-c was associated with changes in folate metabolism, purine biosynthesis and AMPK activation. These findings helped establish a scientific basis for further investigation into mitochondrial-derived signalling peptides.

Researchers continue to explore several related questions:

How MOTS-c influences intracellular metabolic pathways

How mitochondrial-derived signals affect gene expression

How cellular responses vary under different metabolic conditions

How MOTS-c relates to skeletal muscle energy utilisation

How its biological activity differs between experimental models

The precise mechanisms, pharmacological characteristics and clinical relevance of MOTS-c remain incompletely understood.

MOTS-c Research Applications

1. Mitochondrial Signalling

MOTS-c offers researchers an opportunity to investigate how mitochondria may influence cellular activity beyond their traditional role in energy production.

Research into mitochondrial-derived peptides is expanding understanding of the relationship between mitochondrial function, gene regulation and cellular adaptation.

2. AMPK and Energy Regulation

AMPK is an important regulator of cellular energy balance. MOTS-c has been investigated in experimental systems involving AMPK-related pathways and changes in metabolic activity.

This research may help laboratories explore the molecular mechanisms involved in energy sensing and metabolic regulation.

3. Glucose Metabolism and Insulin Signalling

Preclinical research has investigated MOTS-c in relation to glucose utilisation and insulin sensitivity.

The original 2015 study reported that MOTS-c treatment improved measures associated with insulin resistance and diet-related obesity in mice. These findings established an important foundation for further research.

However, animal findings do not demonstrate that administering MOTS-c produces equivalent benefits in humans. Its potential role in human glucose regulation remains unestablished.

4. Skeletal Muscle Metabolism

Skeletal muscle plays a major role in whole-body glucose utilisation and energy metabolism.

Researchers have investigated MOTS-c in relation to muscle metabolic activity and physiological adaptation. This work has generated interest in the relationship between mitochondrial signalling and the regulation of skeletal muscle energy pathways.

Further research is required to establish the relevance of these findings to human physiology.

5. Metabolic Stress and Cellular Adaptation

MOTS-c is also being investigated for its potential involvement in cellular responses to metabolic stress.

Understanding these mechanisms may help researchers examine how cells adapt to changes in energy availability and metabolic demand.

These investigations remain part of an evolving scientific field rather than an established clinical application.

6. Ageing and Metabolic Research

Mitochondrial function and metabolic regulation can change with age. Researchers are therefore investigating whether mitochondrial-derived peptides contribute to age-associated physiological changes.

MOTS-c has attracted interest in this field because of its reported relationship with metabolic homeostasis in preclinical models.

It has not been established that taking MOTS-c slows ageing, extends lifespan or prevents age-related disease.

What Does the Research Say?

MOTS-c research includes cellular experiments, animal studies and human observational research. The strength of evidence varies considerably between these areas.

Preclinical Findings

A foundational study published in Cell Metabolism in 2015 identified MOTS-c as a mitochondrial-derived peptide and investigated its effects on metabolic homeostasis.

In experimental models, researchers reported changes associated with AMPK signalling, insulin sensitivity and diet-related obesity.

These findings provide a basis for continued investigation into mitochondrial-derived peptides and their potential involvement in metabolic regulation.

Human Research

Human studies have examined naturally occurring MOTS-c concentrations in blood and their relationships with metabolic characteristics.

However, observational measurements of naturally occurring MOTS-c are not equivalent to clinical trials in which participants receive manufactured MOTS-c.

The available evidence does not establish the safety, effectiveness or clinical benefits of administering native MOTS-c to humans.

Scientific Limitations

Important questions remain regarding MOTS-c's biological mechanisms, pharmacokinetics, dose-response relationships, potential adverse effects and long-term safety.

Accordingly, claims that MOTS-c is a proven weight-management, anti-ageing, performance-enhancing or metabolic treatment are not supported by established human clinical evidence.

Research References

1. Lee et al. (2015) — MOTS-c and Metabolic Homeostasis

Title: The mitochondrial-derived peptide MOTS-c promotes metabolic homeostasis and reduces obesity and insulin resistance.

Journal: Cell Metabolism, 21(3), 443–454.

DOI: 10.1016/j.cmet.2015.02.009

This foundational study characterised MOTS-c and investigated its relationship with metabolic regulation, AMPK-associated signalling and insulin sensitivity in experimental models.

Read the study on PubMed

2. Kim and Ristow (2015) — Mitochondrial Signalling and Metabolism

Title: A mitochondrially encoded hormone ameliorates obesity and insulin resistance.

Journal: Cell Metabolism.

DOI: 10.1016/j.cmet.2015.02.013

This accompanying research article discusses the potential significance of MOTS-c in mitochondrial signalling and metabolic regulation.

Read the study on PubMed

3. MOTS-c and Muscle and Fat Metabolism

Title: MOTS-c: A novel mitochondrial-derived peptide regulating muscle and fat metabolism.

This review examines the emerging research surrounding mitochondrial-derived peptides and their potential roles in skeletal muscle and metabolic biology.

Find the publication on PubMed
